title: Composition
summary: Assemble behavior by holding objects; inherit only when the type truly is-a subtype.

body:
Rule. Prefer composition: a type holds collaborators and delegates. Use inheritance only when the subtype truly is a specialized kind of the parent and can substitute everywhere the parent is expected (Liskov). Composition keeps coupling local and avoids brittle base classes.

Why it matters. Deep inheritance trees freeze decisions and break when subclasses override half the base. Interviews reward "has-a" designs that inject dependencies. Inheritance remains fine for shallow, stable taxonomies.

Worked example. Bad: class CachedUserRepo extends SqlUserRepo overrides find and secretly caches — callers surprised by stale data and cannot reuse caching for RedisUserRepo. Better: class UserRepoFacade holds a UserRepo port and a Cache; find checks cache then delegates to whatever UserRepo was injected (SQL or Redis). Another: Car has Engine and Wheels rather than inheriting Engine. Testing replaces Engine with FakeEngine. Inheritance that works: Square should not inherit Rectangle if it breaks setWidth assumptions; share a Shape interface instead.  Walk one concrete path with numbers before generalizing. When to use. Use composition as the default for sharing behavior and for swapping collaborators in tests. Use inheritance sparingly for true subtype taxonomies with shared invariants.

When to refuse. Refuse inheriting only to reuse a few helpers — extract a collaborator. Refuse overriding half a base class to cancel its behavior. Refuse deep frameworks of abstract bases when interfaces plus composition suffice. Refuse treating inheritance as the primary reuse tool in greenfield design.
